content: Hepatitis B virus infection represents a significant global health concern. Traditional Chinese medicinal herbs have been extensively utilized in the treatment of chronic liver diseases, and numerous controlled clinical trials have been conducted to evaluate their therapeutic efficacy. The objective of this research was to evaluate both the efficacy and safety of traditional Chinese medicinal herbs in the management of chronic hepatitis B infection. To achieve this, comprehensive searches were conducted across multiple electronic databases, including the Cochrane Hepato-Biliary Group Controlled Trials Register, the Cochrane Complementary Medicine Field Trials Register, the Cochrane Library (Issue 2, 2000), MEDLINE, EMBASE, and BIOSIS (as of October 2000). Additionally, five Chinese journals and conference proceedings were manually searched. Importantly, no restrictions were placed on language during the search process. The inclusion criteria for the trials were as follows: randomized or quasi-randomized trials with a minimum follow-up period of three months. The trials needed to compare Chinese medicinal herbs (either as single agents or in compound formulations) against placebo, no intervention, general non-specific treatment, or interferon therapy. Trials that compared Chinese medicinal herbs combined with interferon to interferon alone were also included. The trials could be conducted in double-blind, single-blind, or unblinded formats. Data extraction was performed independently by two reviewers, and the methodological quality of the trials was assessed using the Jadad scale, supplemented by an evaluation of allocation concealment. Analyses were conducted on an intention-to-treat basis. A total of nine randomized trials, encompassing 936 patients, met the inclusion criteria. However, the methodological quality of these trials was deemed adequate in only one study. A significant asymmetry was observed in the funnel plot (regression coefficient = 3.37, standard error = 1.40, P = 0.047), indicating potential bias. Across the nine trials, ten different medicinal herbs were tested. Among the findings, the herbal compound Fuzheng Jiedu Tang demonstrated significantly positive effects in clearing serum HBsAg, HBeAg, and HBV DNA when compared to non-specific treatment or placebo. Polyporus umbellatus polysaccharide showed significant effects on the clearance of serum HBeAg and HBV DNA. Phyllanthus amarus exhibited a significant effect on serum HBeAg clearance. However, the Phyllanthus compound and kurorinone did not show significant effects on the clearance of serum HBeAg, HBV DNA, or the normalization of alanine aminotransferase levels when compared to interferon therapy. No significant therapeutic effects were observed for the other herbs evaluated in the trials. In conclusion, while some Chinese medicinal herbs may exhibit potential benefits in the treatment of chronic hepatitis B, the current evidence is insufficient to recommend any specific herb for clinical use. There is a pressing need for rigorously designed, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials to establish the efficacy and safety of these treatments.
